call.text: Yes, disguising a thermal detonator as a holocron would be in character for Hux. If the Knights of Ren broke with the First Order and pursued their own agenda, Hux would have every reason to avoid fighting them on their terms. He’s vindictive, willing to deceive his own side, and especially petty where Kylo Ren is concerned. There’s a fitting arrogance in the idea that he thinks he can turn the mystique of the Force against people who take it seriously. It would be a clever move if the Knights already had a reason to want that particular holocron. If they’d been hunting for it because they believed it held a secret Kylo had kept from them, Hux would be exploiting a motive they already had. If he simply assumed any old Sith relic would make them drop their guard, that would be a believable mistake for him. Either version can work, depending on whether you want the scene to showcase his cunning or his contempt. Where Hux puts the fake holocron would determine whether the scene feels earned. Your question cuts off after “putting it on,” so the location is still open. The strongest version would have the Knights come across it in a place the story has already given them a reason to search. That lets them make a sensible choice based on what they know, which makes Hux’s deception more convincing.

My Answer: In natal astrology, Chariklo symbolizes quiet support, compassionate boundaries, and the ability to stay present while someone else finds their footing. Named for the mythological companion of Chiron, Chariklo is often associated with the kind of care that gives people room to heal at their own pace. Her sign can describe how you offer that care, her house can suggest where it comes into play, and close aspects to personal planets can show how it connects with your emotions, relationships, or sense of identity. A recurring challenge is noticing when patience becomes overextension or when keeping the peace keeps you from voicing your needs.

My Conclusion: Chariklo’s central theme is care that leaves room for both people. Her placement can help you reflect on where your presence steadies others and what boundaries help you sustain that generosity.

Future Outlook: Over time, this placement can serve as a prompt to notice when someone needs company, when they need space, and when you need support yourself. Practicing those distinctions can make your relationships more reciprocal.

**One More Star**

I sang one note into the night,
Then sang another, clear and bright.
You asked how long the song could go.
I said, “Pick any number that you know.”

Add one more beat, add one more bar,
Count one more light beyond that star.
However far you count, there’s always one more.
That’s what forever means in this song.

I can hold a tune (and in that tune [a beat {and in that beat (a breath [before the next note])}]),
But I can’t hear all the notes at once.
I know the rule that carries us along.
I can’t picture the whole unending song.

Add one more beat, add one more bar,
Count one more light beyond that star.
My voice will tire, my breath will go,
And still there’ll be another note.

A reasonable originalist reading gives a former president protection against criminal prosecution for exercising powers the Constitution commits exclusively to the President. For other official acts, the stronger originalist case is for a defense tied to the particular statute and presidential function. The Supreme Court adopted a broader rule in *Trump v. United States*, 603 U.S. 593 (2024).

The argument starts quickly with Article II. The Constitution’s grant of exclusive power supplies a bridge from presidential authority to a defense against prosecution. Congress cannot use a criminal statute to punish a President for lawfully granting a pardon. That principle does not transform everything done through the executive branch into constitutionally protected conduct.

The Impeachment Judgment Clause expressly contemplates criminal liability after impeachment and conviction. Its text supplies no bridge to a requirement that the Senate convict before prosecutors may proceed. In *Federalist No. 69*, Hamilton distinguished the President’s accountability through ordinary criminal proceedings from the British king’s inviolability. The historical evidence on the precise treatment of official acts is less abundant. Even abundant evidence against royal immunity would leave open how a court should apply a particular criminal statute when it burdens a presidential power.

Outside the President’s exclusive powers, the prospect of chilling official decisions warrants careful review. It provides a weaker bridge to a general presumption of immunity. On this originalist reading, a court should work through the statute and the constitutional function at issue. Abundant evidence that a President acted through official channels can establish the capacity in which the President acted. It does not, by itself, transform an objection to applying a particular statute into immunity from prosecution.

The *Trump* majority used separation of powers as a bridge to broader protection, reasoning that the prospect of punishment through a later prosecution could distort decisions in office. Its holding gives a former president absolute immunity for acts within exclusive constitutional authority, at least presumptive immunity for other official acts, and no immunity for unofficial acts. To overcome the presumption, the government must show that applying the criminal prohibition poses no danger of intrusion on executive authority and functions. Courts may not classify an act as unofficial by examining presidential motive. The decision also restricts prosecutors from using evidence that probes protected official acts as a bridge to proving charges based on unofficial conduct. Those rules govern a prosecution as it proceeds through the courts.
